claim: Current models of scene processing in the human brain include three scene-selective areas: the parahippocampal place area (or the temporal place areas), the retrosplenial cortex (or the medial place area), and the transverse occipital sulcus (or the occipital place area).
source: Current models of scene processing in the human brain include three scene-selective areas: the parahippocampal place area (or the temporal place areas), the restrosplenial cortex (or the medial place area), and the transverse occipital sulcus (or the occipital place area).
evidence: This is a statement about existing models in the field, supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: At least one other scene-selective site can be detected within the human posterior intraparietal gyrus.
source: Here, we challenged this model by showing that at least one other scene-selective site can also be detected within the human posterior intraparietal gyrus.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from multiple experiments showing scene-selective activity in PIGS.

claim: The posterior intraparietal gyrus scene-selective (PIGS) site was detected consistently in a large pool of subjects (n = 59; 33 females).
source: Despite the smaller size of this site compared to the other scene-selective areas, the posterior intraparietal gyrus scene-selective (PIGS) site was detected consistently in a large pool of subjects (n = 59; 33 females).
evidence: This claim is supported by data collected across multiple experiments with 59 subjects total.

claim: The reproducibility of PIGS was tested based on multiple criteria, including comparing the results across sessions, utilizing different scanners (3T and 7T) and stimulus sets.
source: The reproducibility of this finding was tested based on multiple criteria, including comparing the results across sessions, utilizing different scanners (3T and 7T) and stimulus sets.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 which tested reproducibility across sessions and scanners.

claim: PIGS is significantly sensitive to ego-motion in scenes, distinguishing its role from other scene-selective areas.
source: Furthermore, we found that this site (but not the other three scene-selective areas) is significantly sensitive to ego-motion in scenes, thus distinguishing the role of PIGS in scene perception relative to other scene-selective areas.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from Experiment 6 showing differential response to coherently vs. incoherently changing scenes.

claim: fMRI has been used for many decades to localize cortical regions preferentially involved in scene perception in human and non-human primates.
source: In human and non-human primates (NHPs), fMRI has been used for many decades to localize the cortical regions that are preferentially involved in scene perception (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998; Tsao et al., 2008; Rajimehr et al., 2009; Nasr et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature in the field.

claim: Early studies focused mainly on larger activity sites that were more easily reproducible across sessions and individuals, ignoring smaller sites.
source: Early studies focused mainly on larger activity sites that were more easily reproducible across sessions and individuals, ignoring smaller sites that were not detectable in all subjects and/or were not reproducible across scan sessions, based on the techniques available at that time.
evidence: This is a statement about historical methodological approaches in the field, based on established knowledge.

claim: Three scene-selective areas have been identified in human visual cortex with possible homologs in non-human primates.
source: These models suggested three scene-selective areas within the human visual cortex, with possible homologs in NHPs (Nasr et al., 2011; Kornblith et al., 2013; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The human cortical areas were originally named parahippocampal place area (PPA), retrosplenial cortex (RSC), and transverse occipital sulcus (TOS) based on local anatomical landmarks.
source: The human cortical areas were originally named parahippocampal place area (PPA) (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998), retrosplenial cortex (RSC) (Maguire, 2001), and transverse occipital sulcus (TOS) (Grill-Spector, 2003), based on the local anatomical landmarks.
evidence: This is a historical statement about nomenclature, supported by citations.

claim: Subsequent studies noticed discrepancy between the location of functionally defined areas and anatomical landmarks, leading to renaming as temporal place area (TPA), medial place area (MPA), and occipital place area (OPA).
source: However, subsequent studies noticed the discrepancy between the location of these functionally defined areas and the anatomical landmarked, and instead named those regions temporal place area (TPA), medial place area (MPA), and occipital place area (OPA) (Nasr et al., 2011; Dilks et al., 2013; Silson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about nomenclature evolution in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The idea that scene-selective areas are limited to three regions is based largely on group-averaged activity maps generated after applying large surface/volume-based smoothing.
source: The idea that scene-selective areas are limited to these three regions is based largely on group-averaged activity maps, generated after applying large surface/volume-based smoothing to the data from individual subjects.
evidence: This is an inference about methodological limitations in previous studies.

claim: High thresholds in group-averaged data may not have identified smaller scene-selective areas.
source: Thus, though well founded, this approach conceivably may not have identified smaller scene-selective areas (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference about methodological limitations, supported by visual evidence in Figure 1A.

claim: At the single-subject level, multiple smaller scene-selective sites can be detected outside the three main scene-selective areas when drastic spatial smoothing is avoided.
source: However, at the single-subject level, multiple smaller scene-selective sites can be detected outside these scene-selective areas, especially when drastic spatial smoothing is avoided (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating smaller scene-selective sites in individual subjects.

claim: A recent neuroimaging study in non-human primates using high-resolution techniques suggested that scene-selective areas are likely not limited to three sites.
source: This phenomenon is highlighted in a recent neuroimaging study in NHPs (Li et al., 2022) in which the authors took advantage of high-resolution neuroimaging techniques using implanted head coils. Their findings suggested that scene-selective areas are likely not limited to the three expected sites, and that other, smaller, scene-selective areas may also be detected across the brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study in non-human primates.

claim: Multiple previous studies reported indirect evidence for scene and/or scene-related information processing within the posterior intraparietal cortex.
source: We focused our efforts on the posterior portion of the intraparietal cortex mainly because multiple previous studies reported indirect evidence for scene and/or scene-related information processing within this region (Lescroart and Gallant, 2019; Pitzalis et al., 2020; Sulpizio et al., 2020; Park et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At least one additional scene-selective area was found within the posterior intraparietal gyrus, adjacent to motion-selective area V6.
source: Consistent with these studies, we found at least one additional scene-selective area within the posterior intraparietal gyrus, adjacent to the motion-selective area V6 (Pitzalis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from multiple experiments.

claim: PIGS was detected consistently across individual subjects and populations and localized reliably across scan sessions.
source: This site was termed PIGS, reflecting its location (posterior intraparietal gyrus) and function (scene-selectivity). PIGS was detected consistently across individual subjects and populations and localized reliably across scan sessions.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiments 1, 2, and 4 showing consistency across subjects and sessions.

claim: PIGS is distinguished from other scene-selective areas by its distinct location relative to intraparietal sulcus and parieto-occipital sulci and retinotopic visual areas IPS0-4.
source: Besides its distinct location relative to two major anatomical landmarks (i.e., intraparietal sulcus [IPS] and parieto-occipital sulci [POS]) and the retinotopic visual areas (IPS0-4) that distinguishes it from other scene-selective areas (e.g., TOS/OPA and RSC/MPA), PIGS showed sensitivity to ego-motion within naturalistic visual scenes, a phenomenon not detectable in other scene-selective areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical localization data from Experiment 3.

claim: PIGS showed sensitivity to ego-motion within naturalistic visual scenes, a phenomenon not detectable in other scene-selective areas.
source: Besides its distinct location relative to two major anatomical landmarks (i.e., intraparietal sulcus [IPS] and parieto-occipital sulci [POS]) and the retinotopic visual areas (IPS0-4) that distinguishes it from other scene-selective areas (e.g., TOS/OPA and RSC/MPA), PIGS showed sensitivity to ego-motion within naturalistic visual scenes, a phenomenon not detectable in other scene-selective areas.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data from Experiment 6.

claim: When the level of spatial smoothing is relatively low, scene-selective sites other than PPA/TPA, TOS/OPA, and RSC/MPA are detectable across the brain, especially within the posterior intraparietal gyrus.
source: When the level of spatial smoothing is relatively low, scene-selective sites (other than PPA/TPA, TOS/OPA, and RSC/MPA) are detectable across the brain, especially within the posterior intraparietal gyrus (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In all tested individuals in Experiment 1, at least one scene-selective site was detected within the posterior portion of the intraparietal gyrus, close to but outside the POS.
source: In all tested individuals, besides areas RSC/MPA and TOS/OPA, we detected at least one scene-selective site within the posterior portion of the intraparietal gyrus, close to (but outside) the POS.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 1 showing consistent detection across all 14 subjects.

claim: The relative size of PIGS was 73.86% ± 49.01% of RSC/MPA, 28.26% ± 15.67% of TOS/OPA, and 19.45% ± 8.43% of PPA/TPA when measured at p<10–2.
source: When measured at the same threshold levels (p<10–2), the relative size of PIGS was 73.86% ± 49.01% (mean ± SD) of RSC/MPA, 28.26% ± 15.67% of TOS/OPA, and 19.45% ± 8.43% of PPA/TPA.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from Experiment 1.

claim: The relatively small size of PIGS could not be ascribed to lower signal-/contrast-to-noise ratio in that region considering its proximity to the skull and head coil surface.
source: Considering the proximity of PIGS to the skull and head coil surface (Figure 1), the relatively small size of PIGS could not be ascribed to the lower signal-/contrast-to-noise ratio in that region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical location of PIGS relative to imaging hardware.

claim: PIGS was detectable in group-averaged activity maps in almost the same location as in individual subject maps.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 3A, PIGS was also detectable in the group-averaged activity maps, in almost the same location as in the individual subject maps.
evidence: This claim is supported by group-averaged data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Despite its small size, PIGS is consistently detectable across subjects in the same cortical location.
source: Overall, these results suggest that, despite the relatively small size of this scene-selective site, PIGS is consistently detectable across subjects in the same cortical location.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data from Experiment 1.

claim: Despite utilizing a different scanner (7T vs 3T) and different stimuli, PIGS was still detectable in the same location in Experiment 2.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 4, despite utilizing a different scanner and a different set of stimuli, PIGS was still detectable in the same location (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 2 showing reproducibility across scanners and stimuli.

claim: PIGS was localized within the posterior portion of the intraparietal gyrus and close to the posterior lip of POS in both 3T and 7T scans.
source: Here again, PIGS was localized within the posterior portion of the intraparietal gyrus and close to the posterior lip of POS.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical localization data from Experiment 2.

claim: The higher contrast/signal-to-noise ratio of 7T scans strongly suggested that PIGS evidence was not simply a nuisance artifact in fMRI measurements.
source: Considering the higher contrast/signal-to-noise ratio of 7T (compared to 3T) scans, this result strongly suggested that the PIGS evidence was not simply a nuisance artifact in fMRI measurements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical advantages of 7T scanning and the reproducibility of findings.

claim: Area V6 in the posterior intraparietal cortex is involved in motion coherency (optic-flow) encoding.
source: Posterior intraparietal cortex accommodates area V6, which is involved in motion coherency (optic-flow) encoding (Pitzalis et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on V6.

claim: Recent studies have suggested that scene stimuli evoke a strong response within V6.
source: Recent studies have suggested that scene stimuli evoke a strong response within V6 (Sulpizio et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The intraparietal cortex accommodates multiple retinotopically organized visual areas including IPS0-4 that are involved in spatial attention control and higher-level object information processing.
source: Moreover, the intraparietal cortex accommodates multiple retinotopically organized visual areas (Swisher et al., 2007), including IPS0-4 that are believed to be involved in spatial attention control and higher-level object information processing (Silver et al., 2005; Konen and Kastner, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that area TOS/OPA overlaps with retinotopic visual areas V3A/B and IPS0 (V7).
source: Previous studies have suggested that the area TOS/OPA overlaps with the retinotopic visual areas V3A/B and IPS0 (V7) (Nasr et al., 2011; Silson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: V6 was localized within the posterior portion of the POS without any overlap between its center and PIGS.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Pitzalis et al., 2010; Pitzalis et al., 2015), V6 was localized within the posterior portion of the POS without any overlap between its center and PIGS.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 3a showing spatial separation between V6 and PIGS.

claim: The probabilistic label for PIGS was localized within the intraparietal gyrus and outside the POS, while V6 was located within the POS.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 5, the probabilistic label for PIGS was localized within the intraparietal gyrus and outside the POS (Figure 5A), while V6 was located within the POS (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by probabilistic mapping data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There was no overlap found between area V6 and areas RSC/MPA and TOS/OPA.
source: We also did not find any overlap between area V6 and areas RSC/MPA and TOS/OPA (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by probabilistic mapping data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Despite low threshold levels (probability >20%), areas PIGS and V6 were located side-by-side without overlapping between their centers.
source: Thus, despite the low threshold level used to generate these labels (probability >20%), the areas PIGS and V6 were located side-by-side (Figure 5D), without any overlapping between their centers.
evidence: This claim is supported by probabilistic mapping data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In both subjects in Experiment 3b, PIGS was located adjacent to IPS3 and IPS4.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 6, in both subjects, PIGS was located adjacent to IPS3 and IPS4.
evidence: This claim is supported by retinotopic mapping data shown in Figure 6.

claim: TOS/OPA was located more ventrally relative to PIGS, overlapping with areas V3A/B and IPS0 (V7).
source: In comparison, TOS/OPA was located more ventrally relative to PIGS, overlapping with areas V3A/B and IPS0 (V7).
evidence: This claim is supported by retinotopic mapping data from Experiment 3b.

claim: The differences in localization of PIGS vs. TOS/OPA relative to anatomical and functionally defined landmarks suggest that PIGS and TOS/OPA are two distinct visual areas.
source: Considering these differences in the localization of PIGS vs. TOS/OPA, relative to the anatomical and functionally defined landmarks, our results further suggest that PIGS and TOS/OPA are two distinct visual areas.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical localization data from Experiment 3.

claim: PIGS was detectable in a new population of 31 subjects in almost the same location as in Experiment 1.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 3B, PIGS was also detectable in this new population in almost the same location as in Experiment 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 4 shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PIGS was detected bilaterally within the posterior portion of the intraparietal gyrus, adjacent to the POS in Experiment 4.
source: Specifically, PIGS was detected bilaterally within the posterior portion of the intraparietal gyrus, adjacent to the POS.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 4.

claim: There was no significant difference between the two populations in the size of PIGS when normalized relative to RSC/MPA, TOS/OPA, or PPA/TPA.
source: We did not find a significant difference between the two populations in the size of PIGS when normalized either relative to the size of RSC/MPA (t(43) = 0.98, p=0.33), or TOS/OPA (t(43) = 0.26, p=0.80) or PPA/TPA (t(43) = 0.52, p=0.61).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of data from Experiments 1 and 4.

claim: The location and relative size of PIGS appeared to remain unchanged across populations.
source: Thus, the location and relative size of PIGS appeared to remain unchanged across populations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on comparison of data from Experiments 1 and 4.

claim: ROI analysis using probabilistic labels showed significant scene-selective activity in PIGS (t(31) = 8.11, p<10–8), TOS/OPA (t(31) = 7.91, p<10–7), and RSC/MPA (t(31) = 9.11, p<10–8).
source: As demonstrated in Figure 7A and B, results of this region of interest (ROI) analysis showed a significant scene-selective activity in PIGS (t(31) = 8.11, p<10–8), TOS/OPA (t(31) = 7.91, p<10–7), and RSC/MPA (t(31) = 9.11, p<10–8).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis data from Experiment 4 shown in Figure 7.

claim: The level of scene-selective activity in PIGS was significantly higher than that in V6 (t(11) = 5.03, p<10–4).
source: Importantly, despite the proximity of PIGS and V6, the level of scene-selective activity in PIGS was significantly higher than that in V6 (t(11) = 5.03, p<10–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis data from Experiment 4.

claim: Probabilistically generated ROIs can be used to examine PIGS response and differentiate it from adjacent areas such as V6.
source: Thus, it appears that the probabilistically generated ROIs can be used to examine PIGS response and differentiate it from adjacent areas such as V6 (see also Experiment 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the successful use of probabilistic ROIs in Experiment 4.

claim: The 'scenes vs. objects' and 'scenes vs. faces' contrasts generated similar activity maps in Experiment 5a.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 8B and C for one individual subject, 'scenes vs. objects' and 'scenes vs. faces' (Experiment 4) contrasts generated similar activity maps.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 5a shown in Figure 8.

claim: In both 'scenes vs. objects' and 'scenes vs. faces' maps, PIGS was detectable in a consistent location adjacent to but outside the POS.
source: Importantly, in both maps, PIGS was detectable in a consistent location adjacent to (but outside) the POS.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 5a.

claim: ROI analysis in Experiment 5a yielded significant scene-selective activity within PIGS (t(11) = 6.57, p<10–4), RSC/MPA (t(12) = 11.00, p<10–6), and TOS/OPA (t(12) = 6.26, p<10–3).
source: Moreover, results of an ROI analysis, using the probabilistically generated labels based on the results of Experiments 1 and 3a, yielded significant scene-selective activity within PIGS (t(11) = 6.57, p<10–4), RSC/MPA (t(12) = 11.00, p<10–6), and TOS/OPA (t(12) = 6.26, p<10–3) (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis data from Experiment 5a shown in Figure 9.

claim: In Experiment 5a, the level of scene-selective activity within PIGS was significantly higher than that in adjacent area V6 (t(11) = 2.42, p=0.03).
source: We also found that the level of scene-selective activity within PIGS is significantly higher than that in the adjacent area V6 (t(11) = 2.42, p=0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis data from Experiment 5a.

claim: Scenes and (non-face) objects are differentiable from each other based on the activity evoked within PIGS.
source: Thus, scenes and (non-face) objects are differentiable from each other, based on the activity evoked within PIGS.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data from Experiment 5a showing differential responses.

claim: In Experiment 5b, contrasting response to scene vs. non-scene images evoked a similar activity pattern as scene vs. faces.
source: Despite this change, contrasting the response to scene vs. non-scene images (averaged over objects, scrambled objects, and faces) evoked a similar activity pattern, as scene vs. faces (Figure 8E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 5b shown in Figure 8.

claim: ROI analysis in Experiment 5b yielded significant scene-selective activity within PIGS (t(14) = 2.37, p=0.03), RSC/MPA (t(14) = 10.33, p<10–7), and TOS/OPA (t(14) = 4.79, p<10–3).
source: Moreover, the ROI analysis yielded a significant scene-selective activity within PIGS (t(14) = 2.37, p=0.03), RSC/MPA (t(14) = 10.33, p<10–7), and TOS/OPA (t(14) = 4.79, p<10–3) (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis data from Experiment 5b shown in Figure 9.

claim: In Experiment 5b, the level of scene-selective activity within PIGS was higher than V6 (t(14) = 2.27, p=0.04).
source: Here again, the level of scene-selective activity within PIGS was higher than V6 (t(14) = 2.27, p=0.04).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis data from Experiment 5b.

claim: Results of Experiments 1–5 suggest that PIGS responds selectively to a wide range of scenes compared to non-scene objects, and the level of this activity is higher than in adjacent area V6.
source: Together, results of Experiments 1–5 suggest that PIGS responds selectively to a wide range of scenes compared to non-scene objects, and that the level of this activity is higher than in the adjacent area V6.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data from Experiments 1-5.

claim: The hypothesis that area PIGS is involved in encoding ego-motion within scenes was motivated by the fact that PIGS is located adjacent to V6, an area involved in encoding optic flow.
source: This hypothesis was motivated by the fact that PIGS is located adjacent to V6 (Figure 5D), an area involved in encoding optic flow.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for Experiment 6, based on anatomical proximity and known function of V6.

claim: Other studies have suggested that ego-motion may influence scene-selective activity within the posterior intraparietal region, without clarifying whether this activity was centered within or outside V6.
source: Other studies have also suggested that ego-motion may influence the scene-selective activity within this region, without clarifying whether this activity was centered either within or outside V6 (Pitzalis et al., 2020; Sulpizio et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PIGS showed a significantly stronger response bilaterally to coherently (compared to incoherently) changing scenes that implied ego-motion.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, PIGS showed a significantly stronger response (bilaterally) to coherently (compared to incoherently) changing scenes that implied ego-motion (Figure 11C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 6 supported by data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: The level of activity within RSC/MPA and TOS/OPA did not change significantly between coherently and incoherently changing scene conditions.
source: However, the level of activity within RSC/MPA and TOS/OPA did not change significantly between these two conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 6.

claim: ROI analysis yielded a significantly stronger response to coherently (vs. incoherently) changing scenes in PIGS (t(11) = 5.97, p<10–4) but not in RSC/MPA (t(11) = 0.12, p=0.90) and TOS/OPA (t(11) = 0.48, p=0.64).
source: Consistent with the group-averaged activity maps, results of an ROI analysis (Figure 12) yielded a significantly stronger response to coherently (vs. incoherently) changing scenes in PIGS (t(11) = 5.97, p<10–4) but not in RSC/MPA (t(11) = 0.12, p=0.90) and TOS/OPA (t(11) = 0.48, p=0.64).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis data from Experiment 6 shown in Figure 12.

claim: Area PPA/TPA showed a stronger response to incoherently (compared to coherently) changing scenes (t(11) = 3.48, p<0.01).
source: Interestingly, area PPA/TPA showed a stronger response to incoherently (compared to coherently) changing scenes (t(11) = 3.48, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis data from Experiment 6.

claim: One-way repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant effect of area on the evoked differential activity to 'coherently vs. incoherently changing scenes' (F(3, 11) = 53.89, p<10–10).
source: To better clarify the difference between scene-selective areas, we repeated this test by applying a one-way repeated measures ANOVA to the differential response to 'coherently vs. incoherently changing scenes', measured across these four scene-selective areas. This test yielded a significant effect of area on the evoked differential activity (F(3, 11) = 53.89, p<10–10).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from Experiment 6.

claim: Post hoc analysis with Bonferroni correction showed that the level of differential activity evoked by 'coherently vs. incoherently changing scenes' was significantly higher within PIGS than all other scene-selective areas (p<10–6).
source: Post hoc analysis, with Bonferroni correction, showed that the level of differential activity evoked by 'coherently vs. incoherently changing scenes' was significantly higher within PIGS than all other scene-selective areas (p<10–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical analysis of data from Experiment 6.

claim: The results suggest a distinctive role for area PIGS in ego-motion encoding, which differentiates it from other scene-selective areas.
source: These results suggest a distinctive role for area PIGS in ego-motion encoding, which differentiates it from the other scene-selective areas.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data from Experiment 6.

claim: The absence of activity modulation in other scene-selective areas ruled out the possibility that activity increase in PIGS was simply due to attentional modulation during coherently vs. incoherently changing scenes.
source: The absence of activity modulation in the other scene-selective areas also ruled out the possibility that the activity increase in PIGS was simply due to attentional modulation during coherently vs. incoherently changing scenes (see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results across scene-selective areas in Experiment 6.

claim: Area V6 showed a significantly stronger response to coherently (rather than incoherently) changing scenes (t(11) = 3.57, p<0.01).
source: In addition to PIGS, we also found a significantly stronger response to coherently (rather than incoherently) changing scenes in area V6 (t(11) = 3.57, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis data from Experiment 6.

claim: The level of ego-motion selectivity was significantly weaker in V6 compared to that in PIGS (t(11) = 2.63, p=0.02).
source: However, the level of this selectivity was significantly weaker in V6 compared to that in PIGS (t(11) = 2.63, p=0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of data from Experiment 6.

claim: In group-averaged activity maps, the contrast between coherently vs. incoherently changing scenes yielded a stronger response outside (rather than inside) the POS and also in area MT.
source: Moreover, in the group-averaged activity maps, the contrast between coherently vs. incoherently changing scenes yielded a stronger response outside (rather than inside) the POS and also in area MT, located at the tip of medial temporal sulcus (Figure 11C).
evidence: This claim is supported by group-averaged data from Experiment 6 shown in Figure 11C.

claim: The impact of ego-motion on scene processing is stronger in PIGS than that in V6.
source: Together, these results suggest that the impact of ego-motion on scene processing is stronger in PIGS than that in V6.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of data from PIGS and V6 in Experiment 6.

claim: ROI analysis of response to radially moving vs. stationary concentric rings did not yield any strong (significant) motion-selective activity within PIGS (t(11) = 1.84, p=0.10), RSC/MPA (t(11) = 1.97, p=0.08), PPA/TPA (t(11) = 1.93, p=0.08), and V6 (t(11) = 2.03, p=0.07).
source: Consistent with the previous studies of motion perception (Pitzalis et al., 2010; Korkmaz Hacialihafiz and Bartels, 2015), the results of an ROI analysis here did not yield any strong (significant) motion-selective activity within PIGS (t(11) = 1.84, p=0.10), RSC/MPA (t(11) = 1.97, p=0.08), PPA/TPA (t(11) = 1.93, p=0.08), and V6 (t(11) = 2.03, p=0.07).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis data from Experiment 6.

claim: Strong motion selectivity was found within area TOS/OPA (t(11) = 4.57, p<10–3), likely due to its overlap with motion-selective area V3A/B.
source: In contrast, we found strong motion selectivity within area TOS/OPA (t(11) = 4.57, p<10–3), likely due to its overlap with the motion-selective area V3A/B (Nasr et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis data from Experiment 6 and inference based on known overlap with V3A/B.

claim: In contrast to optic flow and ego-motion, simpler forms of motion only evoke weak-to-no selective activity within PIGS and V6.
source: Thus, in contrast to optic flow and ego-motion, simpler forms of motion only evoke weak-to-no selective activity within PIGS and V6.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of responses to different motion types in Experiment 6.

claim: Biological motion evoked a stronger response bilaterally within area MT and superior temporal sulcus but not within the posterior intraparietal gyrus.
source: As illustrated in Figure 13, and consistent with the previous studies of biological motion (Puce et al., 1998; Beauchamp et al., 2003; Puce and Perrett, 2003; Pelphrey et al., 2005; Jastorff and Orban, 2009; Kamps et al., 2016), biological motion evoked a stronger response bilaterally within area MT and superior temporal sulcus but not within the posterior intraparietal gyrus.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 7 shown in Figure 13 and citations to previous studies.

claim: ROI analysis showed no significant difference between response to biological vs. translational motion within PIGS (t(11) = 1.27, p=0.23), TOS/OPA (t(11) = 1.63, p=0.13), RSC/MPA (t(11) = 1.40, p=0.18), and PPA/TPA (t(11) = 0.41, p=0.69).
source: Consistent with the maps, an ROI analysis (based on the functionally defined labels) showed no significant difference between the response to biological vs. translational motion within PIGS (t(11) = 1.27, p=0.23), TOS/OPA (t(11) = 1.63, p=0.13), RSC/MPA (t(11) = 1.40, p=0.18), and PPA/TPA (t(11) = 0.41, p=0.69).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROI analysis data from Experiment 7.

claim: PIGS does not respond to all types of complex motion.
source: These results indicated that PIGS does not respond to all types of complex motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data from Experiment 7 showing lack of response to biological motion.

claim: Selective scene processing is not limited to areas PPA/TPA, RSC/MPA, and TOS/OPA, and additional smaller scene-selective sites can be found across the visual system.
source: These data suggest that selective scene processing is not limited to areas PPA/TPA, RSC/MPA, and TOS/OPA, and that additional smaller scene-selective sites can also be found across the visual system.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on all experimental data.

claim: Inclusion of PIGS in models of scene processing may clarify how ego-motion influences scene perception.
source: By focusing on one small scene-selective site, we showed that this site (PIGS) was consistently identifiable across individuals and groups. We also showed that inclusion of this site in the models of scene processing may clarify how ego-motion influences scene perception.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ego-motion findings from Experiment 6.

claim: Early fMRI studies dealt with considerable noise in measurements, partly due to using lower magnetic field scanners and imperfect hardware and software.
source: The early fMRI studies dealt with a considerable amount of noise in measurements, partly due to using lower magnetic field scanners and imperfect hardware and software.
evidence: This is a statement about historical limitations in fMRI methodology based on established knowledge.

claim: Noise in measurements affected the reliability of findings in early fMRI studies, causing those studies to focus on larger activity sites.
source: This noise in measurements affected the reliability of the findings. Consequently, those early studies focused on larger activity sites that were more reliably detectable across subjects/sessions.
evidence: This is an inference about how methodological limitations influenced research focus.

claim: Smaller sites in early fMRI studies were either ignored or eliminated by excessive signal smoothing applied to enhance contrast-to-noise ratio.
source: The smaller sites were either ignored or eliminated by excessive signal smoothing, applied to enhance the level of contrast-to-noise ratio.
evidence: This is a statement about methodological practices in early fMRI studies based on established knowledge.

claim: Advances in neuroimaging techniques have made it possible to detect and distinguish fMRI activity at the spatial scale of cortical columns.
source: However, advances in neuroimaging techniques have now made it possible to detect and distinguish fMRI activity at the spatial scale of cortical columns (Yacoub et al., 2007; Zimmermann et al., 2011; Nasr et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous technical studies.

claim: A spatially confined but extensively repeated evoked response can be detected reliably across different sessions.
source: Although the reliability of the fMRI signal still depends on the number of trial repetitions, a spatially confined, but extensively repeated, evoked response can be detected reliably across different sessions (Nasr et al., 2016a; Kennedy et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PIGS could be localized consistently across multiple subjects and across different sessions and scanners.
source: The present data shows that PIGS could be localized consistently across multiple subjects and across different sessions and scanners.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiments 1, 2, and 4.

claim: Probabilistic labels generated based on one population can be used to localize PIGS and distinguish its function from adjacent regions in a second population.
source: Furthermore, our results indicated that the probabilistic labels, generated based on one population, can be used to localize PIGS and distinguish its function from the adjacent regions (e.g., V6) in a second population.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful use of probabilistic labels in Experiments 4 and 5.

claim: The results highlight the reliability of current fMRI techniques in detecting smaller cortical regions at the level of individual subjects.
source: Together, these results highlight the reliability of current fMRI techniques in detecting smaller cortical regions in the level of individual subjects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: To establish a true category-selective response, the stimulus set should sample enough variety to reflect the range and variability among category members.
source: To establish a true category-selective response, the stimulus set should sample enough variety to reflect the range and variability among the category members.
evidence: This is a statement about methodological principles in category-selective research.

claim: Five different scene stimulus sets were tested across experiments, including a wide variety of indoor/outdoor and natural/manmade scenes.
source: Accordingly, here we tested five different scene stimulus sets across our experiments, including a wide variety of indoor/outdoor and natural/manmade scenes.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design across multiple experiments.

claim: In all cases with different scene stimulus sets, a selective response was evoked within PIGS, and the level of this response was comparable to that in adjacent scene-selective areas RSC/MPA and TOS/OPA.
source: In all cases, we were able to evoke a selective response within PIGS, and the level of this response was comparable to that in the adjacent scene-selective areas RSC/MPA and TOS/OPA.
evidence: This is a summary of findings across multiple experiments testing different stimulus sets.

claim: The scene-selective response in PIGS appeared not to be limited to a single subset of scenes.
source: Thus, the scene-selective response in PIGS appeared not to be limited to a single subset of scenes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the variety of scene stimuli tested.

claim: It remains unclear whether scene stimuli are differentiable from each other based on the pattern of evoked response in PIGS.
source: However, it remains unclear whether scene stimuli are differentiable from each other based on the pattern of evoked response in this region.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation and area for future research.

claim: PIGS and TOS/OPA are two distinct scene-selective areas based on multiple criteria.
source: Our results clearly showed that PIGS and TOS/OPA are two distinct scene-selective areas based on multiple criteria:
evidence: This is a conclusion based on anatomical and functional data from multiple experiments.

claim: Anatomically, TOS/OPA is located mostly anterior to the IPS, whereas PIGS is located more dorsally and posterior to the IPS.
source: first, anatomically, TOS/OPA is located mostly anterior to the IPS, whereas PIGS is located more dorsally and posterior to the IPS.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical localization data from multiple experiments.

claim: TOS/OPA overlaps with areas V3A/B and IPS0, whereas PIGS was located adjacent to IPS3-4.
source: Second, TOS/OPA overlaps with areas V3A/B and IPS0, whereas PIGS was located adjacent to IPS3-4.
evidence: This claim is supported by retinotopic mapping data from Experiment 3b.

claim: TOS/OPA and PIGS respond distinctly to moving stimuli, with TOS/OPA responding selectively to moving concentric rings and less selectively to ego-motion, while PIGS shows the opposite pattern.
source: Third, these two areas respond distinctly to moving stimuli. Specifically, while TOS/OPA responds selectively to moving concentric rings and less selectively to ego-motion, PIGS shows the opposite pattern and responds selectively to ego-motion within the naturalistic scenes but not to moving rings (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 6 comparing responses to different motion types.

claim: Considering anatomical and functional differences, PIGS and TOS/OPA appear to be two distinct hubs within the scene processing networks.
source: Considering these anatomical and functional differences, these two areas appear to be two distinct hubs within the scene processing networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined anatomical and functional evidence.

claim: PIGS is located relatively far from the lateral place memory area (LPMA), which is located anterior to the IPS and close to the tip of the superior temporal sulcus.
source: Also notably, PIGS is located relatively far from the lateral place memory area (LPMA), which is located anterior to the IPS and close to the tip of the superior temporal sulcus (Steel et al., 2021; Steel et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with anatomical location of LPMA from cited studies.

claim: Considering the distance from LPMA and the fact that there was no memory demand in the paradigms, PIGS and LPMA appear to be two distinct visual areas.
source: Considering this, and the fact that there was no memory demand in our paradigms, PIGS and LPMA also appear to be two distinct visual areas.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical separation and functional differences.

claim: Ego-motion can significantly influence the activity evoked within PIGS, distinguishing its role in scene perception relative to other scene-selective regions.
source: Our results (Experiment 6) suggest that ego-motion can significantly influence the activity evoked within PIGS. This phenomenon distinguishes the role of PIGS in scene perception, relative to other scene-selective regions.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on data from Experiment 6.

claim: Previous studies have shown that PPA/TPA and RSC/MPA show weak-to-no sensitivity to motion per se.
source: Specifically, previous studies have shown that PPA/TPA and RSC/MPA show weak-to-no sensitivity to motion per se (Korkmaz Hacialihafiz and Bartels, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Area TOS/OPA shows a stronger motion-selective response, presumably related to its partial overlap with area V3A/B.
source: In comparison, area TOS/OPA shows a stronger motion-selective response, presumably related to its (partial) overlap with area V3A/B (Tootell et al., 1997; Nasr et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and inference about the functional consequence of anatomical overlap.

claim: The ego-motion-related activity within PIGS is stronger than in TOS/OPA.
source: Instead, the current data show that the ego-motion-related activity within PIGS is stronger than in TOS/OPA.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 6.

claim: PIGS is located adjacent to area V6, an area that contributes to encoding optic flow.
source: This finding is consistent with the fact that PIGS is located adjacent to area V6 (Figures 4 and 5), an area that contributes to encoding optic flow (Pitzalis et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data from Experiment 3 and citation about V6 function.

claim: Hypothetical inputs from V6 may contribute to the strong ego-motion selective response in PIGS.
source: Considering PIGS and V6 proximity, hypothetical inputs from V6 may contribute to the strong ego-motion selective response in PIGS.
evidence: This is speculation about potential neural mechanisms based on anatomical proximity.

claim: The role of PIGS differs from that in V6 in terms of ego-motion encoding.
source: This said, the current data also suggests that the role of PIGS differs from that in V6 in terms of ego-motion encoding.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of PIGS and V6 responses in Experiment 6.

claim: PIGS contributes to scene encoding and ego-motion within scenes, while V6 is likely involved in detecting optic flow caused by ego-motion.
source: Thus, PIGS contributes to scene encoding and ego-motion within scenes, while V6 is likely involved in detecting optic flow caused by ego-motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion about functional roles based on data from Experiments 3 and 6.

claim: PIGS and TOS/OPA are located on two different sides of the IPS with TOS/OPA located more ventrally compared to PIGS.
source: We showed that PIGS and TOS/OPA are located on two different sides of the IPS with TOS/OPA located more ventrally compared to PIGS.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical localization data.

claim: There is a stronger impact of ego-motion on activity within PIGS compared to TOS/OPA.
source: We also showed a stronger impact of ego-motion on activity within PIGS compared to TOS/OPA.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 6.

claim: TOS/OPA (but not PIGS) responded selectively to simpler forms of motion.
source: In contrast, TOS/OPA (but not PIGS) responded selectively to simpler forms of motion.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 6 testing response to moving rings.

claim: PIGS and TOS/OPA are likely two different visual areas, with PIGS being involved in encoding higher-level ego-motion cues.
source: These results suggest that PIGS and TOS/OPA are likely two different visual areas, with PIGS being involved in encoding higher-level ego-motion cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential response patterns in PIGS vs TOS/OPA.

claim: Kamps and colleagues showed increased response in TOS/OPA during ego-motion vs. static scene presentation.
source: Specifically, Kamps and colleagues have shown increased response in TOS/OPA during ego-motion vs. static scene presentation (Kamps et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Jones et al., 2023 showed that ego-motion (and not other types of movements) enhances TOS/OPA activity when compared to scrambled scenes.
source: Jones et al., 2023 have also shown that ego-motion (and not other types of movements) enhances TOS/OPA activity when compared to scrambled scenes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The current tests showed weak-to-no ego-motion-related activity enhancement in area TOS/OPA.
source: In contrast to these findings, our tests showed weak-to-no ego-motion-related activity enhancement in area TOS/OPA.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 6.

claim: Methodological discrepancies may explain the difference between current findings and previous studies regarding TOS/OPA response to ego-motion.
source: This difference may well reflect methodological discrepancies.
evidence: This is speculation about reasons for discrepancies with previous studies.

claim: In the study by Kamps et al., static and ego-motion stimuli were presented with two different refresh rates, while in the current study, coherently and incoherently changing stimuli were refreshed with the same temporal frequency.
source: Specifically, in the study by Kamps et al., the static and ego-motion stimuli were presented with two different refresh rates. While in our study, the coherently and incoherently changing stimuli were refreshed with the same temporal frequency (see 'Methods').
evidence: This is a comparison of methodological details between studies.

claim: In the study by Jones et al., 2023, the response to scrambled scenes was used as a control condition, whereas the current stimuli were more equivalent, differing only in sequence of image presentation.
source: In the study by Jones et al., 2023, the response to scrambled scenes was used as a control condition, whereas our stimuli were more equivalent, differing only in the sequence of image presentation.
evidence: This is a comparison of methodological details between studies.

claim: Previous studies used higher levels of spatial smoothing (FWHM = 5 mm) compared to the current study during preprocessing.
source: Moreover, these studies used higher levels of spatial smoothing (FWHM = 5 mm) compared to the values we used here during preprocessing.
evidence: This is a comparison of methodological details between studies.

claim: Previous studies limited their analysis to previously known scene-selective areas for understandable reasons.
source: Also, for understandable reasons, they limited their analysis to previously known scene-selective areas.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope of previous studies.

claim: Technical differences make it difficult to directly compare the current results with previous studies.
source: These technical differences make it difficult to directly compare the two sets of results.
evidence: This is an inference about the impact of methodological differences on comparability.

claim: Coherently changing scenes may attract more attention compared to incoherently changing scenes.
source: It could be argued that coherently changing scenes attract more attention compared to incoherently changing scenes.
evidence: This is acknowledgment of an alternative explanation that is then addressed.

claim: The hypothesis that attention differences explain PIGS activity appears consistent with the expected contribution of intraparietal cortex in controlling spatial attention.
source: On the face of it, this hypothesis appears to be consistent with the expected contribution of the intraparietal cortex in controlling spatial attention (Behrmann et al., 2004; Szczepanski et al., 2010).
evidence: This is acknowledgment of how an alternative explanation relates to known functions, supported by citations.

claim: If attention to scenes increased, it should also increase the level of activity within scene-selective areas.
source: But if true, attention to scenes should also increase the level of activity within the scene-selective areas (O'Craven et al., 1999; Nasr and Tootell, 2012b; Baldauf and Desimone, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference about expected consequences of attention, supported by citations.

claim: No significant activity increases were found in response to coherently (vs. incoherently) changing scenes in PPA/TPA, RSC/MPA, and TOS/OPA.
source: While here, we did not find any significant activity increases in response to coherently (vs. incoherently) changing scenes in PPA/TPA, RSC/MPA, and TOS/OPA.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 6.

claim: Modulation of attention, per se, could not be responsible for the enhanced activity within PIGS in response to coherently (compared to incoherently) changing scenes.
source: Thus, modulation of attention, per se, could not be responsible for the enhanced activity within PIGS in response to coherently (compared to incoherently) changing scenes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pattern of results across scene-selective areas.

claim: The stimuli used in coherently vs. incoherently changing block conditions represented the same scenes, with the only difference being the sequence of images within blocks.
source: Furthermore, the stimuli used in coherently vs. incoherently changing block conditions represented the same scenes, and the only difference between the two conditions was the sequence of images within the blocks.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design in Experiment 6.

claim: The two experimental conditions (coherently vs. incoherently changing scenes) may be considered to have the same visuospatial context.
source: In that sense, the two experimental conditions may be considered to have the same visuospatial context.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the experimental manipulation.

claim: Coherently changing scenes may provide more information about environmental layout.
source: However, it could be also argued that the coherently changing scenes provide more information about the environmental layout.
evidence: This is acknowledgment of an alternative explanation.

claim: Previous reports suggest that PPA/TPA and RSC/MPA are involved in layout encoding.
source: In that case, considering the previous reports that PPA/TPA and RSC/MPA are also involved in layout encoding (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998; Wolbers et al., 2011), we expected to see more activity within those regions in response to coherently compared incoherently changing scenes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the absence of activity modulation in PPA/TPA and RSC/MPA, a change in visual context could not be responsible for the enhanced PIGS activity.
source: In the absence of such an activity modulation, a change in the visual context could not be responsible for the enhanced PIGS activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results across scene-selective areas.

claim: Motion-selective sites are expected to show at least some level of sensitivity to motion direction.
source: Motion-selective sites are expected to show at least some level of sensitivity to motion direction (Albright et al., 1984; Zimmermann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about expected properties of motion-selective areas, supported by citations.

claim: The sensitivity of PIGS to the direction of ego-motion was not tested in the current study.
source: We did not test the sensitivity of PIGS to the direction of ego-motion.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the current study.

claim: Pitzalis et al., 2020 showed evidence for motion direction encoding within the V6+ region.
source: However, Pitzalis et al., 2020 have shown evidence for motion direction encoding within the V6+ region (Pitzalis et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Tootell et al. reported evidence for motion direction (approaching vs. withdrawing) encoding within posterior intraparietal cortex.
source: Furthermore, Tootell et al. reported evidence for motion direction (approaching vs. withdrawing) encoding within posterior intraparietal cortex (Tootell et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Previous studies raised the possibility that PIGS may contribute toward encoding ego-motion direction and higher-level cognitive concepts such as detecting intrusion to personal space.
source: Although none of these studies showed any evidence for a new scene-selective area, they raised the possibility that PIGS may also contribute toward encoding ego-motion direction, and even higher-level cognitive concepts such as detecting an intrusion to personal space (Holt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about potential functions of PIGS based on related findings in the literature.

claim: Many past studies have scrutinized the response function of scene-selective areas to numerous stimulus contrasts.
source: In the past, many studies have scrutinized the response function of scene-selective areas to numerous stimulus contrasts.
evidence: This is a statement about the history of research in the field.

claim: Scene-selective areas can differentiate many object categories based on low-, mid-, and/or higher-level visual features according to previous studies.
source: According to these studies, scene-selective areas can differentiate many object categories based on their low-, mid-, and/or higher-level visual features such as their natural size (Konkle and Oliva, 2012), (non-)animacy (Yue et al., 2020; Coggan and Tong, 2023), rectilinearity (Nasr et al., 2014), spatial layout (Harel et al., 2013), orientation (Nasr and Tootell, 2012a), spikiness (Coggan and Tong, 2023), location within the visual field (Levy et al., 2001), and spatial content (Bar et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The current findings are only a first step toward characterizing PIGS in greater detail.
source: Our findings are only a first step toward characterizing PIGS in greater detail.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the scope and limitations of the current study.

claim: More tests are required to reach the current (yet incomplete) knowledge about the response function of PIGS.
source: More tests are required to reach the current (yet incomplete) knowledge about the response function of PIGS.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Neuroimaging studies of scene perception have typically focused on linking scene perception to evoked activity within PPA/TPA, TOS/OPA, and RSC/MPA.
source: Neuroimaging studies of scene perception have typically focused on linking scene perception to the evoked activity within PPA/TPA, TOS/OPA, and RSC/MPA.
evidence: This is a statement about the focus of previous research in the field.

claim: Other scene-selective sites are detectable across the visual cortex but are largely ignored because of their relatively small size.
source: Although other scene-selective sites are detectable across the visual cortex, they are largely ignored because of their relatively small size.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations in previous research approaches.

claim: Future inclusion of small scene-selective sites in models of scene perception may help clarify current models of scene processing in dynamic environments.
source: Our data suggests that the future inclusion of these small sites in the models of scene perception may help clarify current models of scene processing in dynamic environments.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the findings for future research.

claim: Fifty-nine human subjects (33 females), aged 22–68 y, participated in this study.
source: Fifty-nine human subjects (33 females), aged 22–68 y, participated in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: All subjects had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and radiologically normal brains, without any history of neuropsychological disorder.
source: All subjects had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and radiologically normal brains, without any history of neuropsychological disorder.
evidence: This is a description of inclusion criteria for study participants.

claim: All experimental procedures conformed to NIH guidelines and were approved by the institutional review board of Massachusetts General Hospital (2018P001557).
source: All experimental procedures conformed to NIH guidelines and were approved by the institutional review board of the Massachusetts General Hospital (2018P001557).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from all subjects before the experiments.
source: Written informed consent was obtained from all subjects before the experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical procedures in the study.
